unit.title: Rhetorical & Literary Devices
unit.subtitle: Metáfora, ironía, lítotes, metonimia and reading figurative Spanish

grammar.title: Naming the tricks a great writer plays
grammar.intro: At C2 you don't just understand Spanish — you notice how it means. Literary and rhetorical figures bend words away from their literal sense: a metáfora equates two things, lítotes praises by denying the opposite, metonimia names the author for the work. Learn to spot and name each one, and you read the way an educated native reads: between the lines.

sections.heading: Metáfora vs símil
sections.body: A símil compares openly with como or cual (“tus ojos son como el mar”). A metáfora drops the link word and simply identifies one thing with another (“tus ojos son el mar”). The metaphor is bolder: it asserts an equivalence rather than a resemblance.

sections.heading: Hipérbole, ironía, lítotes
sections.body: Hipérbole exaggerates for effect (“te lo he dicho mil veces”). Ironía says the opposite of what is meant, cued by tone. Lítotes (understatement) affirms by negating the contrary: no está mal often means “it's excellent”, and no es tonto means “he's sharp”. To read them you must weigh tone against the literal words.
conj: means the opposite of the words
a softer word for a harsh thing

ex.en: The exam wasn't bad at all. (= it went great)

ex.es: ¡Qué puntual! — al que llega una hora tarde.
ex.en: How punctual! — to someone an hour late.

sections.heading: Metonimia y personificación
sections.body: Metonimia names a thing by something closely linked to it: leer a Cervantes (his works), ganó el oro (the medal), toda la ciudad lo sabe (its people). Personificación lends human action to the inanimate: la tarde agonizaba. Both ask you to supply the real referent the word only points at.

ex.es: En casa leemos mucho a García Márquez.
ex.en: At home we read a lot of García Márquez.
The wind whispered among the pines.

sections.heading: Anáfora y retruécano
sections.body: Anáfora repeats the same word at the start of successive clauses to hammer a point (“Aquí vivió, aquí soñó, aquí murió”). A retruécano reverses the order of two ideas to flip the sense — the famous “¿Siempre se ha de sentir lo que se dice? ¿Nunca se ha de decir lo que se siente?” These are the flourishes of trained rhetoric.

ex.es: Ni están todos los que son, ni son todos los que están.
ex.en: Not all who are, are here; nor are all who are here, all there is.
ex.note: retruécano: the clauses mirror and invert

takeaways: Símil compares with como/cual; metáfora identifies with no link word.
Lítotes affirms by negation: ‘no está mal’ can mean ‘it's excellent’.
Metonimia names by association: ‘leer a Cervantes’ = read his works.
Anáfora repeats an opening word; retruécano inverts two clauses to flip the sense.

mistakes.w: Taking ‘no es tonto’ literally as ‘he is not stupid’ (neutral).
mistakes.r: Reading ‘no es tonto’ as lítotes = ‘he's actually very clever’.
mistakes.why: Understatement negates the opposite to intensify praise, not merely to deny.

mistakes.w: Calling ‘tus ojos son como estrellas’ a metáfora.
mistakes.r: It's a símil — the ‘como’ makes the comparison explicit.
mistakes.why: A metáfora drops como and asserts identity; with como it is a símil.

mistakes.w: Reading ‘se bebió toda la botella’ as literally eating glass.
mistakes.r: It's metonimia: the container (botella) stands for its contents (the wine).
mistakes.why: Metonymy names one thing by something adjacent to it.

exercises.prompt: “Sus ojos eran dos luceros en la noche.” ¿Qué figura es?
exercises.prompt_en: “Her eyes were two bright stars in the night.” Which device is it?
exercises.no: There is no ‘como’; the eyes are directly identified with stars → metáfora.

exercises.prompt: Tras un concierto genial, un crítico dice: “No está nada mal.” Interpretas que…
exercises.prompt_en: After a superb concert a critic says “It's not bad at all.” You interpret that…
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! La lítotes elogia negando lo contrario.
exercises.no: This is lítotes: negating ‘malo’ actually intensifies the praise — it was excellent.

exercises.prompt: Build: "At home we read a lot of Cervantes."
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Metonimia: el autor por su obra.
exercises.no: “En casa leemos mucho a Cervantes” — the author's name stands (metonymically) for his books.

exercises.prompt: Repetir “verde que te quiero verde” al inicio de cada verso es una ___.
exercises.prompt_en: Repeating the same word at the start of each line is called (a)…
exercises.hint: The device of repeating an opening word across clauses.
exercises.ok: ¡Bien! La repetición inicial es la anáfora.
exercises.no: Repeating the opening word across lines is anáfora.

exercises.prompt: Match each device to its defining trait.
pairs: human traits given to a thing
a gentler word for a harsh idea

exercises.tts: El tiempo devora hasta los recuerdos más queridos.
accepted: el tiempo devora hasta los recuerdos mas queridos
exercises.translation: Time devours even the dearest memories.
exercises.no: It was: “El tiempo devora hasta los recuerdos más queridos.” (time is personified).

exercises.scenario: In a literature seminar, dissecting a poem 📖

lines.speaker: Profesora
lines.es: En “sus manos eran hielo”, ¿qué recurso identifica el poeta?
lines.en: In “her hands were ice”, what device does the poet use?

options.text: Es una metáfora: iguala las manos con el hielo sin “como”.
Es un símil, porque compara con la palabra “como”.
Es una hipérbole, porque exagera un número.

exercises.no: There's no ‘como’ and no exaggerated number; the direct identity makes it a metáfora.

exercises.say: Esa ironía esconde una crítica muy afilada.
exercises.en: That irony hides a very sharp criticism.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the rhythm of “Esa ironía esconde una crítica muy afilada.”
